implementation_notes: TypeScript chains are written by hand, but the type system can keep every link honest: returning this (the polymorphic this type, TypeScript 1.7) preserves the concrete class through inherited steps, and a builder that returns a new instance per step can thread accumulated type parameters so the result type reflects the steps actually taken - the shape Kysely and Drizzle use for fluent query builders. Prefer the mutable this-returning form for short-lived configuration you assemble and consume in one place, and the immutable generic form when a partially built chain must be stored, forked or shared: each step then returns a new builder, so a base query can be reused. What replaces the classic structure: an options object typed as a Partial/config interface when the steps are just settings, and generic type parameters when the chain's result depends on which steps ran.
code_sketch:
class Builder { timeout(ms: number): this { this.ms = ms; return this } }   // polymorphic this
class AdminBuilder extends Builder { admin(): this { this.isAdmin = true; return this } }
new AdminBuilder().timeout(10).admin();              // chain keeps AdminBuilder, not Builder

db.selectFrom('person').select(['id', 'name']).where('id', '=', 1).execute();  // new builder per step
pitfalls: A step that declares an explicit widened return type (Builder instead of this) silently truncates the chain in subclasses; use the polymorphic this type or a self type parameter.
Accumulating row types across steps costs compiler time and inference depth: long generic chains need escape hatches ($castTo, explicit type arguments) and can slow the IDE noticeably.

Mutating this-returning builders return the same object, so two variables taken from one base builder alias each other and a step added through either appears in both; immutable chains are the fix when that matters.

variants.name: Immutable chain threading accumulated type parameters
variants.implementation_notes: A step returns a new builder instance whose type parameters describe what has been added so far, so a chain can be stored and forked without aliasing and the terminal call's result type is computed from the steps that ran: `class Query<Table, Row = never> { select<C extends keyof Table>(cols: C[]): Query<Table, Row | Pick<Table, C>> }`. Conditional and mapped types (TypeScript 2.8) do the accumulation, and libraries such as Kysely expose exactly this shape. Choose it when queries/builder values are composed across functions or reused as a base for several chains; accept the extra allocations and the compiler-time cost of heavy generics.
variants.idiom_name: select<C extends string>(cols: C[]): Query<Row | Pick<Table, C>>
pitfalls: Type-level accumulation makes long chains hard to read in error messages and can exceed the checker's inference depth; break the chain with an explicit type argument or a helper function once it grows.
Each step allocates a new builder object, which is wasteful in hot loops; hoist a partially built base and clone from it deliberately instead of chaining inside the loop.
